items.title: Harold Ousley interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001
items.q: But it was always a good place, and Papa Jo would be there.

ctx.x: Yeah. Well musicians who had been in New York would come back to Chicago and tell us about all the wonderful things happening in New York, who they saw, and at this particular time, 52nd Street was the street that was going as well as Minton’s uptown. And these were the musicians we used to listen to on the records, so we were always, you know, open ears and say well we’ve got to go to New York. And I finally got the opportunity through a friend of mine, a trumpet player who moved to Cleveland. And there was a…

pay as much as record dates, but a lot of times you might be able to do five or six demo dates in a day so that was, you know, good money. So you would go in from one bar to another and see who you could find. It was like a networking, like here you just went around to see, you know, no telling who you might run into. But everybody used to go to The Turf or either there was Beefsteak Charlie’s. Now Beefsteak Charlie’s was the place where Milt Hinton and a lot of the musicians who were playing a lot of the better…

That’s interesting. I mean they’re still doing similar stuff today, with people shopping their wares, but this would be something you’d go in, and — how did the music actually come together for those things that quickly?
